Kanji (漢字) are Japanese pictorial characters that were imported from Chinese. Unlike hiragana and katakana, each kanji has a meaning (or several related meanings) and can have different readings.

Basic kanji are arranged in thematic categories from easy to difficult: numbers, common counters, calendar (day, week, month, year), clock and time, directions and sizes, colors, first grade, people and family, nature, food and drink, animals and basic verbs. You can change the category later or add a new category.
Each category has a table with the columns "Kanji itself, Kunyomi (Hiragana), Onyomi (Katakana), Meaning, Example (Kanji), Hiragana and Example meaning"; Each example is displayed in a separate row.
Don't memorize kanji alone; Learn each kanji along with one of its examples. Kanji that repeat in multiple categories are more for review.
After each category, close the table and try to remember the reading and meaning; The more you try to remember, the stronger the memory becomes.
Click on any kanji to copy it to the clipboard.
The Konyomi column is written in Hiragana and the Onyomi column is written in Katakana.
The order of categories is based on difficulty level; If you want a category or kanji, say so that it will be added.

Kanji are the meaningful characters of the Japanese language. Each kanji can form a word by itself (eg 山 = mountain) or combine with other kanji to form a new word (eg 山川 = mountain and river, 火山 = volcanic mountain). The number of kanji used daily is about 2000, of which about 1000 are enough for normal conversation.
It is recommended to start learning with kanji that you see a lot in everyday life: numbers, days of the week, time and directions.
Each kanji has two main readings:
Old Japanese reading of the character, before the introduction of Chinese
Reading the Chinese character that came to Japan with the word

For this reason, in the tables of this page, Kunyumi is written with Hiragana and Onyomi with Katakana to make their difference clear. If a kanji has multiple readings, they are all separated by ・ (for example, 日 has the readings ひ・か in Kunyomi and ニチ・ジツ in Onyomi). Some kanji have only one reading; In this case, you will see the same value.

Japanese grammar is summarized in ten short sections: from sentence order and basic particles to adjectives, the て form, order of events, and comparison. Each topic has a title and exactly two real examples to review at a glance. All examples are written in hiragana and katakana only, so they are readable with knowledge of hiragana and katakana page.
Click on any Japanese example to copy it to the clipboard.
The particles は and へ are not read in the writing of ‌ha and ‌he; They are pronounced "Wa" and "E" respectively.
All forms are "polite" (ていねい) and are used in everyday conversation, school and work.
The backbone of every Japanese sentence: the order of the blocks, the particle that tells the role of the noun, and the particle that makes the sentence a question.
Sentence order: The verb always comes last
The three particles に, で and へ are the most used in everyday sentences; Especially the difference between に (time) and で (place).
I wake up at seven o'clock.
I study from nine to five.
We make a noun phrase with です; の joins two nouns together and も takes the place of は to say "both".
The stem of the verb remains the same and only the ending (ます) changes: it makes tense, negation, and invitation.
I will go to Tokyo tomorrow.
Aren't you going to see a movie tomorrow? (invitation)
い adjectives are used by themselves, な adjectives behave like nouns and come before nouns with な.
To be in Japanese has two verbs: ショット for inanimate things and コッド for animate things; Counting is also done with a counter.
There is a book on the table.
There is a cat in the room.
My friend is at the station.
desire, interest, ability and permission; Four patterns that are repeated the most in conversation.
I want to go to Japan.
Can I take a photo here?
Section 8 - Form of て and sentence linking
The て form is the gateway to advanced grammar: with it we connect sentences, make requests, and tell the state or current action.
I wake up in the morning and eat.
I go to the library and study.
I am reading a book now.
I will not go because it is raining.
Because it is cold, I close the window.
To say "before", "after", "when" and "at the same time", the base verb comes in the simple form and the pattern comes after it.
I read a book before going to bed.
I wash my hands before eating.
I watch a movie after work.
I listen to music when I am idle.
I played a lot as a child.
I study while listening to music.
The last step of the summary: comparing two things, the best choice, wanting something and giving a personal opinion.
I like winter more than summer.
The train is faster than the bus.
The highest mountain in Japan is Fuji.
I think it will rain tomorrow.
Part I - Basic Sentences and Everyday Questions

This section is based on the beginning lessons of the books みけれの にほんご, Marugoto A1 and Japanese for Busy People: from the simple pattern "A は B です" and the particle の to pointing with こ・そ・あ・ど, short questions and answers, numbers and everyday questions such as price, age, name, ownership and time.
In this section, all examples are written only with hiragana and katakana.
The particle は is pronounced "wa" and the particle を is pronounced "he"; Click on any sample to copy it.
To ask "How much?" We are dealing with いずつ and for the price with キラ.
1. Pattern A は B です
The simplest Japanese sentence is made of two nouns and です: "A は B です" means "A is B". は indicates subject/subject role and です makes a polite tone.
Mr. Mailer is an employee of the company.
I am a Japanese language teacher.
Mr. Mailer is not a student.
2. The particle の — possession and connection
の joins two nouns together: "the second noun of the first noun". The same particle makes possession, category and type, and can take the place of a noun ("property of...").
Linking two nouns - category, type and dependency
That person is a Japanese language teacher.
Belonging to... — の without a noun
This book belongs to the teacher.
3. Hint: こん・ここ・ここ
All the sign words fit into a grid of four: こ for something close to the speaker, そ for something close to the listener, あ for far from both, and ど for a question.
On the other side is the bathroom.
The office is on the other side.
Every news sentence is questioned with か. The short answer comes with はい / いいえ and if we don't understand the sentence, we ask to repeat it with a short phrase.

I don't understand — request to repeat

Excuse me, what did you say?

Second part - verb, particle and time (lessons 6 to 12)

From this part, sentences are made with verbs: present group, particle that illuminates the role of the noun, time and negation, presence and count. The order of the contents is the same as the order of lessons 6 to 12 of the book みこんの日本語 1.
The verb always comes at the end of the sentence; Every noun that comes before the verb is followed by a particle.
The ます form is polite and is used in class, at work, and with strangers.
1. Three groups of verbs and form ます
All Japanese verbs fall into three groups. We know the group from the simple form (辞書形) and this group determines how the form ます is made.
The last letter from line う goes to line い of the same row and gets ます: のむ → のみ + ます.
Only る is removed and ます is added.
Although the verb いく (to go) ends in る, it belongs to Group 1: いく → いききが.
The four tenses of ます
I go to school every day.
2. Particles を, に, で and へ
The four particles that carry the most semantic load of the sentence: subject, destination and time, place of work and direction.
Both に and へ are correct with verbs of motion (いか, くる, かえる).
- Place of work, tools and language
に is for "being" and で is for "doing".
The ending まます with ままた and まませ makes tense and negative; か also makes the sentence a question.
I saw my friend last week.
In the short answer, the main verb is repeated: はい、ままう / いいえ、みしまたた.
4. Existence: あります and います
To be in Japanese has two verbs: ショット for inanimate things and コッド for animate things. The place of the thing comes with に and the thing itself comes with が.
There are thirty students in the class.
It is in front of the bank station.
There is a bag under the table.
In Japanese, each category of things has its own counter. The counter comes after the number and before the verb and changes depending on the voice.
The order of the sentence does not change: subject + を + number + counter + verb.
6. Interest and skill: すき・きらい・じょうず・へた
These four words are adjectives and their object comes with が. For intensity, とん and ぜんぜん (with negative) are used.
The child does not like meat.
To describe another じょうず, we usually use とくい (dominant) for ourselves.
7. Wanting: たいです and なるすです
たい is used to want to do something and なるる is used to want something; Both are used like the adjective い.
I want to come back early tomorrow.
Negative: たくくいです, Past: たるかつ, Negative Past: たくなりたでで.
To ask for a job from another: 〜てくるすです (fourth part).
8. Invitation: ままますか and ままますか
Three forms for proposal and invitation. Their difference is in the level of politeness and whether we propose the work ourselves or with the other party.
This form is more polite than ましょう, because it gives the other person a choice.
The て form is the gateway to Japanese grammar: with it we connect sentences, make requests, ask permission, and express mood.
Memory rule: て-form for う・つ・る "って", for む・ぶ・ぬ "んて", and the rest take their row sound.
10. おます — current work and state
With the form て + いまて, we say two things: an action that is going on right now, and a state that continues for some time.
In Persian, it is sometimes translated as "I live" and sometimes as "I am married"; Both have the same pattern.
11. Permits and prohibitions: てななりです / てはいけません
To ask permission and say prohibition, the form て is combined with ななわ and はいけません.
Positive answer: はい、いいです／またる. Polite negative answer: すみません、します…
12. から・まで・ごろ・さんで・だだ
These five words make interval, approximation and limitation and are very widely used in everyday conversation.
I will be back around three o'clock.
It is about a thousand yen.
ごろ for time, アプレ for quantity and duration.
In this section, all the necessary patterns for the JLPT N5 exam and the end of the book みこんの日本語 1 are gathered: ない form, た form, conditional, comparison, quotation, reason and polite request.
Before each pattern, know the simple form of the verb (辞書形／ない形／た形); Most models ride on the same.
In compound sentences, the following clause always comes before the main clause and the main verb is the last.
Practice the patterns in this section together; For example, たら + アック + いともいまて makes a natural sentence.
1. The five forms of て: てから, てみる, てかる, ててる, てある
These five patterns are the most used in conversation and each one creates its own exact meaning.
After eating breakfast, I go to school.
I left my umbrella in the train.
The book is placed on the table.
てある comes with a transitive verb and the particle が; かかか with the necessary verb and the particle が: まどが しまきますます
ない is a simple negative form and the basis of three important patterns: must, don't need and don't.
ending in line あ + ない
I have to study every day.
You don't have to come tomorrow.
3. Simple form (辞書形) and its uses
The simple form is the one that comes in the dictionary and comes before the patterns こと, まえに and おますと.
I read a book before going to sleep.
I wash my hands before eating.
I am saving money to go to Japan.
I walk every day for health.
For nouns: 〜のために; for verbs: 〜るために.
4. Form た — experience, arrangement and novelty
The た form is the simple past tense and forms three usage patterns: experienced, after doing, and just finished.
I have the experience of climbing Fuji.
I have cooked Japanese food before.
For negative experience: 〜たことがありません.
With the name: 〜のあとで; With verb: 〜たあとで.
たします is "low" in terms of the speaker, not in terms of the clock.
5. ながら — at the same time as
It connects two simultaneous tasks; The main work comes in the final sentence.
The subject of both actions is the same: わたしは おんがくを ききばあら べんきょうします
6. とき and あいだ — time
とる is used for "when" and あいだ for "in the interval of time".
I studied a lot when I was a student.
When I go to Japan, I buy a camera.
Before きろ: adjective な + な, noun + の, simple form verb.
The cat was sleeping until I was gone.
I read a book while riding the train.
あいだ = throughout that period; あいだに = at some point in that interval.
7. Basic conditional: と and たら
N5's most used biconditional: と for natural result and たら for general "if/when".
When spring comes, the flowers open.
By pressing this button, the door opens.
と is usually not followed by a personal request or intention.
I will not go if it rains.
I will call when I get home.
If it is cheap, I will buy it.
The adjective い becomes く and the adjective な becomes に; We say spontaneous change with なる and created change with する.
Four patterns of comparison: より, のなんな, また〜ない and いちばん.
This year is hotter than last year.
The train is more comfortable than the bus.
Today is not as hot as yesterday.
10. Intention and plan: 가이, よてい, いこもいまて
We have three different patterns to say personal plan, definite plan and personal opinion.
I plan to go to Japan next year.
I am not going anywhere tomorrow.
I have a meeting scheduled tomorrow.
I have a travel plan next month.
と is preceded by the simple form of the verb and adjective and the noun + だ.
11. Reason and contrast: から, まて, のに, ける
Four linking words that tell the relationship between two sentences: reason, soft reason, expectation against expectation and speech opposition.
I will not go because it is raining.
Because I don't have time, I go by taxi.
I close the window because it is cold.
I will come back because I have something to do.
Although I studied, I failed the exam.
I work even though it is closed.
It's cold, but I'm going out.
I like it but I don't eat it.
With this, we guess the appearance of a thing; Its form is different from the adjectives い and な.
It looks like it will rain.
Adjective い: い is omitted (おかい → おいしそう). ない → なさそう; いい → よさそう; The adjective な comes unchanged.
13. Giving and receiving: あをる, くれる, もらる
The direction of the gift or service is important: あをる from me to another, くれる from another to me, もらる from me to receive.
I gave a pencil to my new colleague.
I give my friend a book.
My friend gave me a book.
My father gave me a watch.
- I get it from someone else
I got a book from my friend.
I also learned from the teacher.
The teacher corrected it for me.
14. Simple form (普通形) and friendly speech
The simple form is the same without ます and です; In friendly speech, it is used in the following sentence and before patterns.
In simple speech, ててる is shortened to てる: てかる → してる.
With んき, the sentence is explained: the speaker expresses his reason, background or discovery.
what happened - I have a slight fever.
why did you take leave - I had something to do.
Before んき: simple form verb, adjective い, adjective な + な, noun + な.
16. すぎる, やすい and にくい
Three suffixes that attach to the root of the verb or adjective and give a more precise meaning.
I ate too much last night.
This book is easy to read.
17. Polite request: ていただけませんか
In shops, offices and parties these forms are used; more polite than てください.
Can you say it one more time?
Can you write your name here?
18. Guess: でしょう and かもしれません
To express probability, でしょう (high probability) and かもしれません (lower probability) are used.
Part IV - ability, will, condition and direction (Lessons 26 to 38)
At the N4 level, verb forms are expanded: ability, will, indefinite, causal and conditional. This section is where news and official Japanese sentences are made.
All the forms in this section are made from the same root; The complete table is given in the sixth section.
The examples are written in kanji, with the reading of each sentence in romaji below.
Unknown and causal are widely used in news, report and administration; They are less common in everyday speech.
1. Ability: 可能形 and ことができます
To say "I can", the verb is in the form of ability and the object is usually followed by が.
Group 1: ending in line え + る (飲む → 飲める). Group 2: る → エィード する → かるか, 来る → 来らるか.
2. Purpose: ために and ように
two target patterns; The choice between them depends on whether the verb is voluntary or involuntary.
I write in bold so that the child can read.
It is used with わかる, できる, 見える and other involuntary verbs.
3. ようにする and ようになる
One is effort and habit formation, the other is a natural change of ability or state.
I try to exercise every day.
I am used to waking up early every morning.
4. Will: 意温形 and 生おおもいまて
The will form is used for "come...", "I intend to..." and self-suggestion.
I will wake up early tomorrow.
Group 1: ending in line お + う (飲む → 飲もう). Group 2: る → よう. する → えまう, 来る → 来よう.
I am definitely planning to go to Japan this year.
I plan to leave the company.
In an indefinite sentence, the person who did the work comes with に and the subject of the sentence is affected.
Group 1: あ-line + れる (読む → 読かる). Group 2: る → ション. する → 来来 → 来手か.
In Japanese, when something is unpleasant for us, we make the sentence indefinite; In Farsi, it is often translated as "got".
It rained and I got wet.
They built a building next to us and it became crowded.
They kicked my leg in the train.
7. Cause (使役) — to make and allow
When someone leaves or allows someone to do something, the verb takes a causative form.
I let the child play outside.
The teacher makes the student read the book.
Group 1: あ-line + かせ (遊ぶ → 遊ばかせ). Group 2: る → さるか. する → make 来来 → 来ます
8. Causative-anonymous (使役受身) — I had to
The causative and indefinite combination says that someone forced us to do something; In Farsi, "I was forced" or "I was forced".
The teacher made me stand for an hour.
As a child, I had to eat vegetables a lot.
Group 1: あ-line + あるれ. Group 2: る → あるらるか.
general and formal conditional; It is often seen in proverbs and logical sentences.
If you press this button, the door will open.
Group 1: え-line + ば. Group 2: る → てー. する → Adjective い: い → さて. Negative: If not.
10. なら — if the topic is …
Makes an opinion or recommendation based on what the other party has said.
If you are going to Japan, January is good.
If you want sushi, that shop is famous.
confirms the result in any situation; It also comes with nouns and adjectives.
I will go even if it rains.
No matter how much you hurry, you will not arrive.
Even if it is expensive, I will buy it.
Based on the information, we make logical conclusions; Not forced, but expected.
He must have arrived by now.
Such a thing is not possible.
13. Guess and hearsay: ようです, らしい, みたい
Three ways to guess; The difference is in the source of information and the degree of formality.
It seems that there is no one.
They say it will rain tomorrow.
I heard he left the company.
14. そうです — I heard that …
This そうです is different from the appearance そうです (section 3): here we are quoting something from a source.
According to the weather forecast, it will be sunny tomorrow.
Quotations, verbs, and adjectives are preceded by the simple form (not ます).
15. さんーでで — just now, just before, just now
It shows three exact times: before starting, in progress, and just finished.
I want to go out now.
16. ばかり and だけ — only and just now
With the form of た, it makes がこな "fresh" and with the noun "only"; なん is also neuter "only".

Three ways to tell the reason; The difference is whether the result is positive or negative.

brings multiple reasons or features in succession; In Farsi, it is translated as "Ham...Ham..."

3. だけでなく / ばかりでなく — not only …
Adds something: not only A, but B.
He speaks not only English but also Japanese.
This book is not only useful but also interesting.
It maintains a state: in the same state, without changing.

5. うちに — until / in the interval that
We use the limited opportunity of a period; It is often translated as "not yet".
I want to travel a lot until my youth.
Let's go back before it rains.
Every time I go to Japan, I buy souvenirs.

Direct relationship between two values: the more, the more.

8. くらい and ほど — extent and size
They make approximation and intensity; アーズ is more colloquial and more formal.

9. によって / による — depending on, by
Three uses: difference by agent, agent doing the work, and cause.
People have different opinions depending on the person.
This book is written by Murasaki Shikibo.
Position shows the reaction or ratio of something to another thing.
Said a rude word to the teacher.
The answer to this question is one.
It specifies the topic of speech, research or opinion.
What do you think about this issue?
It tells the role or position of someone or something.
He went to Japan as a student.
I took this as a souvenir.
13. さちろか / ここかか — what about
It defies expectation and suggests something greater.
Kanji has its place, hiragana is also difficult for me.
He speaks not only English, but also French.

to talk about the work of elders and clients; The verb is either taken with お/ご or takes a special form.
